Cholesterol Awareness: When Should You Get Tested?

As seasons change and we focus on building healthier habits, keeping an eye on your heart health becomes an essential part of routine self-care. Managing your heart health is one of the simplest yet most important things you can do to protect your overall wellness for years to come.

Many people assume that high cholesterol only affects older adults or individuals who are visibly out of shape. While that is a common belief, the reality of cardiovascular health is a bit more complicated. At First Medical Associates, we want to help you understand when to get tested so you can stay safe, informed, and proactive about your health.

Table of Contents

  1. What Is Cholesterol and Why Does It Matter?
  2. Recommended Ages for Cholesterol Screening
  3. Key Risk Factors That Call for Earlier Testing
  4. What to Expect During a Cholesterol Test
  5. How First Medical Associates Supports Your Heart Health

What Is Cholesterol and Why Does It Matter?

Cholesterol is a waxy, fat-like substance that your liver produces naturally. Your body actually needs some cholesterol to build healthy cells, produce vital hormones, and digest foods properly. However, having too much of it circulating in your bloodstream can create serious health problems.

There are two main types of cholesterol that you need to know about. Low density lipoprotein, often called bad cholesterol, can build up along the inner walls of your arteries. Over time, this buildup forms hard plaque that narrows your blood vessels and restricts blood flow. High density lipoprotein, or good cholesterol, works like a cleanup crew by carrying excess cholesterol away from your arteries and back to your liver. If your bad cholesterol is too high or your good cholesterol is too low, your risk for heart disease and stroke rises significantly.

Recommended Ages for Cholesterol Screening

Because high cholesterol rarely causes any noticeable physical symptoms, getting screened through a simple blood test is the only way to know your numbers. National health guidelines recommend specific testing timelines based on age.

Children and Teens: Current AHA guidance recommends screening between ages nine and eleven for children who have not already been screened. A pediatric clinician can advise on earlier testing or follow-up based on individual risk. First Medical Associates sees and treats adults ages 18 and older; patients under 18 should receive screening and care from a pediatric practice.

Young Adults: Current AHA guidance recommends a cholesterol blood test starting at age nineteen and at least every five years for most adults. Your clinician may recommend more frequent testing based on your risk factors or previous results.

Older Adults: Men aged forty-five to sixty-five and women aged fifty-five to sixty-five should get screened every one to two years. Anyone over sixty-five should have their cholesterol checked annually.

Key Risk Factors That Call for Earlier Testing

There is no single schedule that works for every individual. Your specific testing frequency depends on several unique personal and lifestyle factors.

Family History: If your parents or siblings have a history of high cholesterol or early heart attacks, your provider may recommend starting routine tests much earlier.

Existing Health Conditions: Living with diabetes, high blood pressure, or kidney disease increases your risk of developing heart complications, requiring more frequent screening.

Lifestyle Choices: Eating a diet high in saturated fats, living a sedentary lifestyle, being overweight, or smoking cigarettes can all raise your bad cholesterol levels rapidly.

Previous Abnormal Results: If a past blood test showed elevated cholesterol or triglyceride levels, your doctor will want to check your numbers more frequently to monitor your progress.

What to Expect During a Cholesterol Test

Getting your cholesterol checked is a quick and straightforward process. The test is called a lipid panel or lipid profile, and it measures four key types of fats in your blood: total cholesterol, bad cholesterol, good cholesterol, and triglycerides.

To ensure the most accurate results, your healthcare provider may ask you to fast, meaning you should avoid eating or drinking anything except plain water for eight to twelve hours before your blood draw. The procedure takes only a few minutes, and your results are typically available within a few days. Once the lab processes your sample, your doctor will go over the numbers with you and explain what they mean for your overall health.

How First Medical Associates Supports Your Heart Health

Managing your cholesterol does not have to be confusing or overwhelming. Making simple, heart-healthy swaps in your diet, exercising regularly, and staying on top of routine screenings can make a massive difference in your long-term wellness.

At First Medical Associates, our clinics across Maryland provide care for adults ages 18 and older and can help you monitor and manage your cholesterol. Whether you need a routine lipid panel, guidance on diet and exercise, or help managing a chronic condition, our experienced providers in communities like Rockville, Bowie, and Annapolis are here to help.
